Two critiques followed. They showed that performance on letter-string analogies collapses when the alphabet is permuted or replaced by symbols, while human performance does not. The original authors replied that the failures come from an auxiliary difficulty with counting, and that GPT-4 solves the permuted problems at a human level once it can write and execute code. This paper reads all three rounds in full, including the preprint and published versions of the reply, and sorts their claims into three groups. Settled: the replications agree, and the unaided model fails the counterfactual variants under answer-only prompts. Moved: the evidence. The third round's decisive result is for a model-plus-interpreter system, while its title claim remains about language models. Unsettled: which operations count as auxiliary, and whether the models represent the new alphabet at all. Published checks from both sides, run in different studies with different alphabets, suggest splitting "counting" into two operations: GPT-4 names the one-step successor of a letter in a permuted alphabet almost perfectly, but identifies the interval (of up to two steps) between two given letters about one time in ten. A study of four newer models, however, finds every model worse at naming items two steps away, and its authors conclude that the models do not build representations of novel alphabets on the fly. If the difficulty lies in recognising the relation in the source pair, it lies in what componential theories of analogy call inference; if it lies in representing the order, it lies in encoding, which the same theories also count as part of analogy. On that decomposition, either way, the reply's "auxiliary" label is not yet earned. The paper states a procedure for reading capacity claims from counterfactual tasks, in which the decomposition of the task is fixed before data are seen, and proposes five experiments on existing materials that could decide between the readings. Every number in it is taken, or summed, from the published sources.

This study was designed as a systematic review to identify, critically appraise and synthesise the available evidence concerning throw-ins in association football. The scope of the review was deliberately broad because the existing literature does not treat the throw-in as a single, homogeneous performance variable. Instead, the evidence addresses complementary dimensions ranging from the regulatory and biomechanical constraints of the action to its temporal management, offensive organisation, defensive responses and contribution to subsequent attacking outcomes. Accordingly, the review sought to integrate these dimensions within a single evidence framework while maintaining clear distinctions between technical, tactical, contextual and outcome-related findings. The review was reported in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses 2020 statement (PRISMA 2020; Page et al., 2021), and the identification and reporting of information sources and electronic search procedures were additionally guided by the PRISMA extension for searches (PRISMA-S; Rethlefsen et al., 2021).[KS6.1][DP6.2][Á6.3] The review was structured around an adapted Population–Exposure–Comparator–Outcome framework appropriate for observational and performance-analysis research. The population comprised male and female association-football players and teams across youth, amateur, semi-professional, professional and international competitive contexts; the exposure was a throw-in occurring during association football; comparators, when applicable, comprised alternative technical executions, tactical organisations, contextual conditions or competitive environments; and outcomes encompassed biomechanical, temporal, tactical, possession, territorial, defensive and attacking indicators directly related to throw-ins. The primary research question was: What is known about the technical, temporal, tactical and performance-related characteristics of throw-ins in association football, and which contextual factors appear to influence their effectiveness? Five secondary research questions were specified to reflect the principal thematic structure of the review: (1) What regulatory and biomechanical characteristics define the execution of a throw-in, and which technical factors influence throwing performance? (2) How are throw-ins related to playing time, restart duration and strategic management of match tempo? (3) Which offensive tactical strategies and contextual factors are associated with successful possession retention, progression and attacking outcomes following a throw-in? (4) How do defending teams organise and respond to throw-ins, and which contextual factors influence pressure, recovery and subsequent transitions? (5) What is the contribution of throw-ins to goal scoring and shot creation, both directly and through the subsequent possession? These questions were selected to ensure that the review did not reduce throw-in effectiveness to a single endpoint such as possession or goals. In particular, the review considered that direct goals are a relatively distal and infrequent outcome, whereas first contact, possession retention, territorial progression, shot creation and defensive recovery may represent more sensitive intermediate indicators of performance. The primary objective was therefore to synthesise the evidence across these interconnected levels and determine the practical relevance of the throw-in as a phase of play. The protocol was not prospectively registered. Nevertheless, the review procedures were systematically developed, documented and operationalised throughout the review process. Eligibility criteria, study-selection procedures, data-extraction domains, methodological-appraisal procedures and the synthesis framework were defined and progressively refined prior to their application to the final evidence set, with all decisions documented in the master evidence database to ensure transparency, consistency and reproducibility. 2.2. Eligibility criteria Eligibility criteria were predefined according to the research questions and were applied at both title-and-abstract and full-text screening stages. Population and context Studies were eligible when they examined male or female players or teams participating in 11-a-side association football. Youth, amateur, semi-professional, professional and international competitive levels were eligible. Studies conducted in futsal, beach soccer, rugby, Australian football, Gaelic football, American football, robotic football or other sports or football formats were excluded. Exposure The exposure of interest was a throw-in performed during association football or analysed in a context intended to evaluate its technical, biomechanical, temporal, tactical, defensive or match-performance characteristics. Throw-ins were required either to constitute the primary phenomenon under investigation or to form an independently analysable category within a broader study of match interruptions, set pieces, possession, playing time, passing, defensive behaviour, shot creation or goal-scoring patterns. Studies in which throw-ins were mentioned only incidentally and for which no independently extractable throw-in-specific information was available were excluded. Comparators A formal comparator was not required for descriptive or biomechanical studies. Where comparisons were reported, eligible contrasts included different throwing techniques, directions or distances; quick versus delayed restarts; different pitch zones; different levels of defensive pressure; match periods or score-lines; competitions, teams or competitive levels; and alternative offensive or defensive organisations. Outcomes Eligible studies reported at least one outcome directly related to the throw-in. Outcomes were organised into five prespecified domains corresponding to the research questions: (i) regulatory and biomechanical outcomes, including throwing velocity, distance, release angle, trajectory, spin and technical determinants of execution; (ii) temporal outcomes, including restart duration and contextual variation in the timing of execution; (iii) offensive outcomes, including first-contact success, reception, possession retention and duration, territorial progression, pressure evasion and entry into advanced areas; (iv) defensive outcomes, including pressure type, defensive organisation, ball recovery, counterpressure and subsequent transition behaviour; and (v) attacking end-products, including shot creation, shots on target, goal-scoring opportunities and goals. Studies focused exclusively on motor learning, injury prevention, artificial intelligence, general physical conditioning or unrelated technical skill acquisition were excluded when they did not provide throw-in-specific outcomes relevant to at least one of the five review domains. Conversely, biomechanical or technical studies were eligible when their primary focus was the throw-in itself, because biomechanics constitutes an explicit thematic component of the review. Study design and publication status Eligible designs included observational match analysis, notational analysis, analytical cross-sectional studies, retrospective or prospective performance analysis, longitudinal designs, biomechanical analyses, statistical or causal modelling, and experimental or quasi-experimental studies examining eligible throw-in outcomes. Only full peer-reviewed original research articles were included in the systematic synthesis. Reviews, editorials, commentaries, conference abstracts, theses, dissertations, book chapters, protocols and other non-original publications were excluded from the systematic synthesis. Relevant reviews were not considered eligible studies for the evidence synthesis but were retained as complementary sources for contextualisation and backward and forward citation searching. No publication-year restriction was applied. No language restriction was imposed during the electronic searches; language was subsequently recorded during screening and data extraction. The final body of evidence included in the systematic synthesis comprised English-language publications. 2.3. Information sources and search strategy The definitive electronic searches were conducted from database inception to 6 August 2026 in MEDLINE via PubMed, Web of Science Core Collection, Scopus, and SPORTDiscus with Full Text via EBSCOhost. These databases were selected to provide complementary coverage of biomedical, multidisciplinary, sport-science and performance-analysis literature. The initial search was developed and executed by one author (A.R.), establishing a traceable and reproducible starting point; complementary identification procedures were subsequently undertaken by the review team. An exploratory search was initially performed in PubMed and EBSCOhost using three Boolean formulations designed to maximise sensitivity for literature explicitly addressing throw-ins: (1) ((soccer[Title]) OR (football[Title])) AND (throw-in[Title]) OR (throw-ins[Title]); (2) ((soccer) OR (football)) AND (throw-in) OR (throw-ins); and (3) ((soccer) OR (football)) AND (out-of-bound) OR (out-of-bounds). This exploratory strategy yielded 34 records after duplicate removal and identified four directly relevant studies following title/abstract and full-text screening. The limited yield demonstrated the risk of relying exclusively on highly specific title-based retrieval and motivated expansion of the search to multidisciplinary databases and broader title/abstract/topic fields. The definitive search combined two principal concepts: association football and throw-ins. Objective: The objective of this article is to develop an integrated sociotechnical framework and a diagnostic maturity model for artificial intelligence-driven supply chain due diligence. It addresses the implementation gap under escalating mandatory regulations by demonstrating how technological capabilities, ethical governance, and cultural adaptation interact, shape each other, and must be developed together. Research Design & Methods: We employed a theory-building approach and conducted a purposive literature synthesis. We applied thematic analysis, grounded in institutional theory, stakeholder theory, and the technology-organisation-environment framework to develop an integrated framework and maturity model, illustrated via analysis of European e-commerce sustainability disclosures. Findings: We identified three critical sociotechnical interfaces (tech-ethics, ethics-culture, and tech-culture) and derived three formal propositions from the analysis. We propose, organisational readiness may function more as a coefficient than an additive factor, where the substantive effectiveness of technological tools depends on cultural commitment. A distinct ‘institutional governance gap’ emerges from the illustrative application. Implications & Recommendations: Organisations, including small and medium-sized enterprises and entrepreneurial ventures operating within mandatory due diligence supply chains, should move beyond techno-centric approaches to assess artificial intelligence (AI) readiness simultaneously across operational, institutional, global, and strategic layers. The maturity model enables systematic capability gap identification. Contribution & Value Added: We propose a diagnostic maturity model and formal propositions that bridge the gap between legal theory and organisational implementation. These contributions are conceptual and require empirical validation.

documents.abstract: Abstract Accelerator-based neutrino physics is entering an energy-frontier regime in which interactions reach the tera-electronvolt scale and produce exceptionally dense, overlapping detector signatures. Event interpretation is impractical for conventional reconstruction and challenging for supervised models trained from scratch, particularly when labelled data are scarce and analyses span diverse objectives. Here we present a sparse Vision Transformer framework for learning reusable representations from heterogeneous detector data. Self-supervised pretraining combines masked-autoencoder reconstruction with relational voxel-level objectives for hierarchy, ghost and particle identification, followed by joint fine-tuning across classification and regression tasks. On simulated events from the proposed FASER calorimeter (FASERCAL) concept, pretraining improves neutrino-flavour and charm-quark identification, momentum regression and vertex reconstruction, with relational objectives providing further gains in topologically complex channels. Attribution and representation diagnostics show a more structured latent space, while detector-subsystem ablations recover physically plausible channel-dependent roles. With roughly 10 3 labelled events, the pretrained encoder matches the flavour-classification performance of scratch training with an order of magnitude more data. Cross-domain transfer is observed on public plastic-scintillator and liquid-argon benchmarks. A matched alternative-generator stress test shows stable flavour and kinematic performance while exposing charm tagging as generator sensitive. These results support self-supervised multimodal pretraining as a route towards reusable detector representations. We use ‘foundation-style’ in this restricted sense, rather than claiming a completed general-purpose detector foundation model.
